title: The Uncle Clause
logline: James and Tom's kids request Uncle Barney as their sitter by name, and Barney bets his brother he'll have them asleep by eight thirty. Nine-year-old Ruby, raised by a labor mediator, retains Marshall as counsel, opens bedtime talks at 'Thursday' and takes Barney for his TV, his suit and every Saturday for a year, while the gang's babysitting advice turns out to be their childhoods talking.
coldOpen: Kids, your Uncle Barney once negotiated with Swiss bankers, a Monaco shipping heir and a bouncer in Atlantic City named Tiny. In 2013, he finally met his match.

couch.line: Let me guess. She was gorgeous.
She was nine. And she had a lawyer.

guests.name: Tom
guests.role: James's husband, a labor mediator who has ended three citywide strikes by calmly saying 'I hear you'; warm, unflappable, never raises his voice, and the reason his nine-year-old negotiates like a union boss

scenes.summary: Sharing a cab home from Loretta's birthday lunch, James asks Barney to babysit: the kids requested Uncle Barney by name. Barney vows to beat James's bedtime record of 9:41 with 8:30 sharp; James warns him about Ruby, who negotiated a sitter out of her car and charges a dollar per catchphrase. Ted prescribes a book with no feelings (his parents' bedtime story was their fake marriage); Robin prescribes her father's spark plug. James: this is why the kids didn't ask for them.

beats.line: That spring, four of us shared a cab home from Loretta's birthday lunch.
Why do I always get the hump?
Because seven years ago, Barney told you it was the keystone.
And structurally, he wasn't wrong.
Little brother. Saturday's our anniversary. Tom and I need a sitter.
Say no more. I know a Swedish au pair. Well. She's been to Ikea.
Not her. The kids asked for someone specific.
Uncle Barney.
They requested me?
Ted. I've been requested. Like a power ballad.
How old are these people?
Ruby's nine, Jackson's six. Ruby put the request in writing and underlined it twice.
Jackson voted no. Jackson votes no on everything. He voted no on his own birthday.
Nine and six. Perfect. Old enough to be impressed, too young to see through me.
Little brother, our last sitter left our house without her car.
Ruby stole her car?
No, Ted. Ruby negotiated for it.
I like her already.
Bedtime is eight thirty. Nobody's ever hit it. My personal record is nine forty-one.
Nine forty-one? Amateur. I'll have them asleep at eight thirty. On the dot.
Tom's a labor mediator. Twenty years of settling strikes. Ruby's been taking notes since she was two.
Please. I've closed deals with Swiss bankers.
Ruby made a Swiss banker cry. At brunch. Over a muffin.
Eight thirty, big brother. Challenge—
Careful. Ruby charges a dollar a catchphrase. She's saving up for a jet ski.
Barney, take my advice. Read them a bedtime story. Just not one with a happy ending.
Why not?
Every night, my parents told me a story about how in love they were.
They'd been divorced for a year.
Ted.
In fairness, there were plot holes.
So read them this. Collected Lectures on the Load-Bearing Wall. No plot. No feelings. A wall can't lie to you.
Nobody has ever made it past chapter two.
Dad. Is that the book under our wobbly table?
It's load-bearing, Luke. It always has been.
Forget stories. Discipline. Lights out means lights out.
When I was six, my dad cut the power to the whole cabin at eight sharp.
That's a little intense.
We had a generator. He took the spark plug to bed with him.
I was twelve before I found out other kids got goodnight. My dad said dismissed.
Thank you both. This is exactly why the kids didn't ask for you.

scenes.summary: Saturday. Barney unveils the Sandman play; Lily (never negotiate, never promise; the board game called Pony) and Marshall (his brothers wrestled him to sleep) add their advice. James and Tom drop off the kids, who head straight for the suit room, with Ruby's notarized terms. Barney's first one-sided negotiation through the bedroom door costs him the TV, two scoops, the Stormtrooper's naming rights and Sundays. Ruby requests counsel, and Marshall, the littlest Eriksen, defects to represent the kids; Lily signs on with Barney to beat her husband. Marshall's opening offer on bedtime: Thursday.

beats.line: That Saturday, Barney prepared for babysitting the way other men prepare for a heist.
They requested me, Lily. I'm the Springsteen of uncles. Tonight, I play the hits.
The Sandman. Step six. Collect brother's tears.
beats.title: The Sandman
lines: Laser tag in the hallway. Exhaust the targets.

beats.line: Step three. Warm milk. Barney, your oven is made of cardboard.
That oven isn't for cooking, Lily. It's so women assume I cook.
I have twenty-two five-year-olds every day. Rule one. Never negotiate. The second you negotiate, they smell it.
It's true. I chaperoned one field trip and came home sixty pretzels in debt.
Rule two. Never promise anything you won't deliver.
Every birthday, my dad promised me a pony. Every birthday, I got a board game called Pony.
How was it?
No rules. Just a picture of a pony I wasn't getting.
My advice? Wrestle them. Wear them out. My brothers pinned me every night until I passed out.
Your brothers wrestled you unconscious?
Lovingly. I didn't know you could just go to bed until college.
Little brother. Delivery for Uncle Barney.
Where are they?
They ran right past you. They're in the suit room.
Nobody goes in the suit room!
Barney. I hear you. And that's a valid feeling.
Ruby asked me to give you her terms. She had them notarized.
By who?
Our doorman. He owed her a favor.
Rule one, bedtime is a conversation. Rule two, because I said so is not an argument.
Nine forty-one, little brother.
Eight thirty, big brother.
Ruby. Jackson. Uncle Barney here. Lights out is eight thirty.
Because I said so.
That's in the terms? Who drafted these?
Tom. Of course.
Fine. One episode on the big TV. Then lights out.
Don't you I hear you me, young lady!
Jackson, buddy. Ice cream?
He said no. He's already eating it.
Good news. We have a deal. Lights out, eight thirty.
What did it cost you?
The big TV, two scoops, naming rights to the Stormtrooper, and Sundays.
What about Sundays?
I don't know. She said it so confidently.
Also, she's requested counsel. The big one who cries at cartoons.
She asked for me?
Marshall. Don't you dare.
Lilypad, I was the littlest Eriksen in a house full of giants. Nobody ever represented me.
Marcus used to sit on my chest and call it a verdict.
Marshall Eriksen, if you walk through that door—
Sorry, Lily. The little guy needs a lawyer.
Fine. Barney, you've got counsel. Me.
You said never negotiate.
With children. That's my husband. I've waited my whole marriage for this.
My clients have an opening offer on bedtime.
Let's hear it.
Thursday.

scenes.summary: James and Tom's anniversary dinner. James trades texts with Barney, who swears both kids are asleep at 8:24 and that Ruby's pajama photo is a stock photo. James confesses his real record is 12:40, the night Ruby had the flu, and why he said yes: when they were kids, he was Barney's sitter. Flashback: Staten Island, 1984, twelve-year-old James negotiating bedtime with nine-year-old Barney, and charging extra to wait up. News arrives that Lily is representing Barney and Marshall the kids. Tom offers to go rescue him. James: 'I hear you.' Dessert menu.

beats.line: Across town, James and Tom's anniversary dinner lasted four minutes before James checked his phone.
James. That's the ninth time you've checked your phone.
I'm not checking, Tom. I'm gloating in advance.
That's a stock photo.
beats.title: Barney

messages.text: Both asleep. 8:24. Your record is toast.

beats.line: Eight twenty-four. He's going to beat your record.
He won't. My record isn't nine forty-one.
It's twelve forty. And that was the night she had the flu.
You lied to your brother?
Tom, he's my little brother. Lying to him is how Stinsons say I love you.
Then why say yes? You won't even let my mother babysit.
Your mother tried to put Ruby to bed at seven. Ruby got her to cosign a lease.
James.
Because Barney's done this before. Mom went out a lot. I was twelve. Somebody had to be the grown-up.
James? When's Mom coming home?
Late. Want to negotiate bedtime?
Midnight!
Nine. And I get your allowance.
Eleven. And you play Battleship for real. No letting me win.
Ten. And I sink every ship you've got.
Deal. Will you wait up with me?
Sure. That's another week's allowance.
You charged a nine-year-old to wait up with him?
I was twelve, Tom. I wasn't a saint. I was a sitter.
Ruby says Barney lawyered up. He hired Lily.
Who's representing the kids?
Marshall.
Oh, they're going to destroy him.
Should we go home and rescue him?
Tom. I hear you.
Waiter! The dessert menu, please. All of it.

scenes.summary: Montage of five hours of talks. At 11:50, Barney is in monogrammed silk pajamas, Lily has caved for three scoops, and Ted's book has a reader with notes. Robin notices all their advice was their parents; Marshall notes the one guy with zero parenting is the one the kids asked for. Ruby's final term: a true story about little Barney. Barney realizes she anchored him with everything else. James and Tom slip in as Barney tells the kids about the worst sitter on Staten Island who never let him win and always waited up, and why he knew exactly who to be. Both asleep; Jackson said yes. James reveals the coffee can of allowance; Barney spends it on catchphrases. James's real record was 12:40, so Barney wins by forty-two minutes, in pajamas. Marshall reveals the uncle clause: every Saturday for a year. Future Ted: Ruby finished Ted's book and out-negotiated him too.

beats.line: My clients reject the warm milk. They know about the oven.
Eight thirty! Lights out! Okay, eight forty-five.
Chapter four. The flying buttress. Part two.
Fine! Three scoops! Three!
Lily, you were supposed to be my lawyer.
She cried, Barney. One tear. Perfectly timed. That's not a child. That's a professional.
Barney! Did chapter two work?
Oh my god. He's out of the suit.
Silk. Monogrammed. I'm not an animal.
You look like a magician going through a divorce.
Ruby took the suit at eight sixteen. She said it's a sleepover, not a merger.
And Ted, your book? She made it to chapter nine. She has notes.
Nobody has ever had notes!
Also, I owe her forty-one dollars in catchphrases.
You know what I just realized? All of our advice was just our parents.
I told a grown man to wrestle children unconscious.
And the one guy here with zero parenting is the one they asked for.
Thanks, Marshall.
My clients have one final term. They'll be asleep in five minutes.
In exchange for what?
A true story. About you. When you were little.
I don't do true stories.
We know.
Counteroffer. A mostly true story.
They anticipated that. Ruby says, and I quote, we'll know.
Oh, she's good. TV, ice cream, my suit. Five hours of everything, so the one thing she wanted would feel cheap.
She's nine, and she ran my own move on me. I've never been prouder or more broke.
Shh. Ruby's getting a true story out of him.
That's my girl.
Okay. True story. When I was about your age, Ruby, my mom went out a lot.
Your dad was twelve, and the worst babysitter on Staten Island. He took my allowance. He never let me win. Not once.
And he waited up with me. Every single time.
Here's the thing. Grown-ups who let you win aren't really playing. I always wished I had one who'd play for real.
So tonight, I knew exactly who to be. I've been waiting for him since I was nine.
They're out. And Jackson said yes.
Jackson said yes?
He said no at his own adoption.
How long have you been there?
Since worst babysitter on Staten Island.
Mostly true.
For the record, I never spent your allowance. It's still in a coffee can at Mom's.
Great. That covers the catchphrases.
It's eleven fifty-eight. James, that beats your real record.
Real record?
Twelve forty. You're a Stinson. You should have checked.
Forty-two minutes, big brother. Legendary.
You just suited up in pajamas.
One more thing. Page four. The uncle clause. Every Saturday for a year. You initialed it during the ice cream.
I read that contract!
Lilypad, you were on your third scoop.
Every Saturday. For a year. That's an outrage.
Can I bring the laser tag guns?
Barney. I hear you.
Barney babysat every Saturday that year. He never once got them down by eight thirty, and he never once let them win.
And Ruby's still the only person who ever finished my book. Last year she hired me to design her house. Somehow, I paid her.
